title: Impact of ferrite/martensite interface on nanohardness in a Dual-Phase steel: A combined experimental and theoretical study
abstract: This combined experimental and theoretical study examines the impact of ferrite/martensite (F/M) interface on the hardness/indentation depth curve during nanoindentation tests on a Dual-Phase (DP) steel. Depth-dependent hardness measurements are performed and compared with the classical Indentation Size Effect (ISE), which typically predicts a monotonic decrease in hardness with increasing indentation depth. However, in ferritic regions near martensite, the present experimental investigation reveals a non-monotonic nanohardness behavior with an initial decrease due to the classic ISE, followed by an increase from a critical indentation depth and a final decrease from a second critical depth. The intermediate stage with an increase in nanohardness between these two critical depths indicates a localized hardening mechanism, which is not captured by the classic ISE model equation. Using a large enough dataset of representative indents performed in ferritic grains close to F/M interfaces, the experimental study demonstrates that this localized hardening is attributed to these specific interfaces acting as strong barriers to plasticity. It is also shown that the increase in nanohardness follows a clear power-law dependence on the microstructural surface geometric distance between the indent position and the nearby F/M interface location. A model, based on Strain Gradient Plasticity (SGP) theory, and explicitly accounting for this distance, is used to explain this nanohardness increase and estimate the evolutions of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities between both critical indentation depths at the origin of the pronounced size-dependent strengthening. These results shed new light on the plasticity mechanisms that control hardness variations at the nanoscale in DP steels due to ferrite/martensite interface, and provide a framework for better understanding the effects of phase boundaries on localized plasticity.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In response to growing performance and efficiency requirements, the automotive industry is increasingly adopting materials that combine high strength with high ductility. Third generation Advanced High Strength Steels (AHSS) provide this combination, offering good mechanical properties that contribute to vehicle weight reduction ( Anderson et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2009 ). Among these steels, Dual-Phase (DP) steels are particularly attractive. Their microstructure, made of a soft ferrite matrix and hard martensite islands, gives them an excellent balance of strength, ductility, and formability ( Anderson et al., 2017 ). Many studies have investigated the behavior of DP steels at the microscale using Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) ( Calcagnotto et al., 2010 ), micromechanical modeling ( Ismail et al., 2019 ), crystal plasticity ( Jeon et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024 ), and highlighting various deformation and damage mechanisms ( Li et al., 2019; Delincé et al., 2007; Ramazani et al., 2013; Allain et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2016; Aydiner et al., 2024; Vermeij et al., 2023 ). To fully benefit from DP steels in engineering applications, it is important to understand how their local mechanical response is influenced by microstructural features such as ferrite/martensite (F/M) interfaces.

Nanoindentation is a powerful technique for characterizing the mechanical behavior of different steels ( Delincé et al., 2006; Choi et al., 2009; Chamma et al., 2025 ). One of the most important phenomena observed in nanoindentation is the Indentation Size Effect (ISE), where the hardness increases when the indentation depth becomes very small. Beyond the classical studies on the ISE in metals, recent research has shown that size dependent hardness is a general phenomenon found in many types of materials. Several reviews have re-examined experimental results and various explanations of ISE, pointing out that it remains a complex effect that is still not fully understood ( Pharr et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, studies performed on ceramics, piezoceramics, and metallic glasses have demonstrated that features such as grain size or phase distribution have a strong impact on indentation behavior ( Renjo et al., 2014; Kathavate et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2016 ). Similar trends are observed in multiphase steels, where the small plastic deformation zone and the presence of phase boundaries can lead to non-monotonic hardness changes at very low indentation depths ( Soman et al., 2019; Ekmekci et al., 2023; Basu et al., 2022 ). In Fe–Si bicrystals, it was shown that the formed plastic zone also depends significantly on the type of grain boundary ( Wakeda et al., 2021 ).

At the same time, recent progresses in Strain Gradient Plasticity (SGP) models, including updates to the classic Nix–Gao model ( Nix and Gao, 1998 ), show that microstructural length scales must be included to accurately describe size dependent hardness ( Wang et al., 2025; Haušild, 2021 ). Altogether, these advances highlight the importance of combining experiments and modeling to account for microstructural variations, Geometrically Necessary Dislocation (GND) accumulation ( Nye, 1953; Ashby, 1970 ), and interface effects in complex multiphase materials, such as DP steels. The effect of ISE is mainly caused by the accumulation of GNDs beneath the indenter tip, due to strong plastic strain gradients in the deformed zone ( Nix and Gao, 1998; Begley and Hutchinson, 1998; De Guzman et al., 1993; Ma and Clarke, 1995 ). Classical plasticity cannot describe this behavior because it does not include any material length scale. In contrast, the SGP theory addresses this limitation by introducing a length scale related to GNDs and the associated plastic strain gradients ( Ashby, 1970; Aifantis, 1992; Fleck et al., 1994; Fleck and Hutchinson, 1993; Begley and Hutchinson, 1998; Gao et al., 1999 ). The pioneering model of  Nix and Gao (1998)  established the first clear relation between hardness and indentation depth. This model was later extended to different indenter shapes ( Swadener et al., 2002 ) and refined by accounting for the plastic zone radius ( Feng and Nix, 2004; Durst et al., 2005 ).

In polycrystalline metals, grain boundaries also play an important role in the mechanical response. More recent works have tried to improve the classic Nix–Gao model by explicitly integrating microstructural features into the description of the ISE. Several extensions of the Nix–Gao model have been developed these last decades to describe nanohardness in materials with different grain sizes ( Yang and Vehoff, 2007; Voyiadjis and Abu Al-Rub, 2005; Almasri and Voyiadjis, 2010; Voyiadjis et al., 2010; Voyiadjis and Peters, 2010; Jung et al., 2013; Voyiadjis and Zhang, 2015; Zhang and Voyiadjis, 2016; Voyiadjis and Yaghoobi, 2017; Voyiadjis and Song, 2019 ). For example,  Jung et al. (2013)  modified the Nix–Gao model equation for hardness as a function of indentation with the help of a modified SGP theory to incorporate the grain size of single phase polycrystalline specimen. Their model was validated against the experimental data of  Yang and Vehoff (2007)  for polycrystalline Ni. Using microindentation tests,  Xu et al. (2024)  studied ten two-phase steels with different grain sizes and ferrite fractions (including DP steels) and they showed that the characteristic depth

However, their analysis was only based on Vickers microhardness measurements, which eliminates the possibility to study the specific role of F/M interfaces on nanohardness curves at small depths in comparison with ferrite/ferrite (F/F) interfaces. Using instrumented nanoindentation, it was shown that decreasing grain size in electrodeposited polycrystalline nickel leads to constrained plastic deformation in the grains below the indenter and a progressive deviation from the Nix–Gao model ( Petr et al., 2023 ). In addition to grain size, the effect of irradiation-induced defects on depth-dependent hardness for ion-irradiated nanostructured multilayers/substrate systems was reported by  Liu et al. (2021) . Besides,  Xiao et al. (2017)  proposed a theoretical model describing the non-monotonic hardness–depth response in bicrystals, first incorporating the truncation of the plastic zone beneath the indenter by a perpendicular grain boundary to describe the increase in nanohardness. In addition, to explain the subsequent reduction in hardness, these authors accounted for dislocation transmission through the grain boundary after dislocation pile-ups, as reported earlier by different authors ( Wo and Ngan, 2004; Eliash et al., 2008; Britton et al., 2009 ). This model and the previous ones represent significant advances in understanding indentation size effects in the presence of grain boundaries. However, they have mainly been applied to single phase materials and not to multiphase microstructures, such as those encountered in DP steels for which slip transmission mechanisms at F/M interfaces appear to be more complex.

In DP steels, microstructural features such as grain size, phase distribution, and especially ferrite/martensite (F/M) interfaces strongly affect the indentation response ( Delincé et al., 2006; Choi et al., 2009; Tsipouridis et al., 2011; Ghassemi-Armaki et al., 2014; Seok et al., 2014 ). Such F/M interfaces act as strong barriers to plasticity, where the plastic zone depends on the heterogeneous microstructure as studied with a finite element (FE) model ( Basu et al., 2022 ), leading to local hardening and complex stress and strain fields. Nanoindentation studies on DP steels have shown that hardness does not simply change with depth, but also varies with the distance to the F/M interface ( Delincé et al., 2006; Ghassemi-Armaki et al., 2014 ). Another work based on Vickers microhardness measurements confirmed that grain and phase boundaries strongly increase local hardness following a Hall–Petch type effect owing to GND accumulation ( Tsipouridis et al., 2011 ). Recent studies have provided clear evidence that the F/M interface is a key factor controlling local deformation.  Matsuno et al. (2020)  combined nanoindentation and FE simulations to show that hardness increases when approaching the martensite phase because of plastic deformation incompatibility between ferrite and martensite.  Chang et al. (2021)  studied the hardness profiles for different interfaces including F/M interfaces in the case of a multiphase steel (i.e. a CP800 steel) constituted of three major phases: ferrite, bainite and martensite. Interestingly, they reported that the hardness near F/M interfaces is higher than near ferrite/bainite interfaces. Furthermore, they showed that both phase distribution and interface morphology have a direct impact on local hardening by influencing local GND density accumulation. All these preliminary results demonstrate that the steel microstructure has a strong influence on nanohardness which modifies the classic ISE, especially at small indentation depths where the plastic zone remains confined within heterogeneous regions ( Delincé et al., 2006; Ghassemi-Armaki et al., 2014; Soman et al., 2019; Ekmekci et al., 2023 ). In some study cases for which nanoindentation was performed near interfaces, a three stage response (softening, hardening, and re-softening) was reported ( Almasri and Voyiadjis, 2010; Voyiadjis et al., 2010; Voyiadjis and Peters, 2010; Voyiadjis and Zhang, 2015; Zhang and Voyiadjis, 2016 ). This highlights the need for developing advanced models that couple SGP theory together with microstructural interfaces such as grain or phase boundaries. To address these challenges, the present study combines nanoindentation experiments with a SGP model adapted for a DP steel. Using a Berkovich indenter and continuous stiffness measurement, controlled nanoindentation tests inside ferritic grains and near F/M interfaces were performed. The results reveal strong variations in nanohardness with indentation depth and distance to the F/M interface, including non-monotonic trends that classical theories cannot describe. To interpret these observations, a SGP model inspired from the works of Voyiadjis and co-workers ( Voyiadjis and Peters, 2010; Voyiadjis and Zhang, 2015; Voyiadjis and Song, 2019 ), was used and a microstructural length  
                         l 
                       equal to the measured distance between the indent tip and the nearest F/M interface was introduced in this model. This additional length allows the model to account for GND accumulation at interfaces and provides new insight how F/M interfaces may affect the size dependent hardness of DP steels at small scale. This understanding is essential for the design of new AHSS grades with improved performance and controlled interface properties.

The paper is organized as follows. Section  2  describes the material and the experimental procedures, including sample preparation, SEM/EBSD characterization, and nanoindentation testing procedure. Section  3  presents the experimental findings on microstructural surface geometric distance measurements and nanohardness responses, both far from and near the F/M interfaces. Section  4  described the Strain Gradient Plasticity (SGP) theory, detailing its assumptions, model formulation and parameter identification from comparisons with the experimental results. It is followed by a discussion provided in Section  5 . Finally, concluding remarks and perspectives are drawn in Section  6 .

Backscattered electron (BSE) imaging and EBSD analyzes with Band Contrast (BC) and Band Slope (BS) imaging were performed on the Dual-Phase steel using a JEOL JSM-F100 field-emission scanning electron microscope. SEM and EBSD are complementary techniques that, together, provide detailed information on the microstructural and crystallographic characteristics of the material. SEM offers high-resolution imaging and compositional contrast through backscattered electrons, whose intensity increases with atomic number, enabling the visualization of compositional variations across the surface. In contrast, EBSD provides local crystallographic orientation and phase information by analyzing Kikuchi diffraction patterns generated when the tilted crystalline sample interacts with the electron beam. Hence, by combining BSE (SEM) and BC (EBSD) imaging, it is possible to visualize the spatial arrangement of ferrite and martensite phases and to accurately locate nanoindentation sites relative to phase boundaries. As shown in  Fig. 6 , an indent located far away from F/F and F/M interfaces provides a measure of the intrinsic hardness of the ferrite, without significant influence from nearby ferritic or martensitic grains. The indentation process induces the formation of mobile dislocations, which initially propagate with little resistance due to the absence of strong obstacles in the surrounding ferritic matrix. Nevertheless, the ferritic grains under investigation are not free of pre-existing dislocations (cf.  Fig. 2 ). With ongoing plastic deformation, the dislocation density around the indent increases, leading to a reduction in the average spacing between dislocations. This promotes mutual interactions and hinders dislocation mobility. The degree of dislocation interaction, combined with the resistance imposed by the crystal lattice, governs the local deformation behavior under the applied loading conditions.

sections.heading: Nanohardness responses in ferritic grains near F/M interfaces
paragraphs: Fig. 7  presents the nanohardness curves as a function of the indentation depth near F/M interfaces for eleven grains (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J and K) investigated in  Figs. 4 and B.15 . The results show non-monotonic nanohardness evolution. All the curves indeed exhibit a local increase followed by a gradual decrease as the indentation depth increases. It clearly contrasts with the cases of nanoindentation within ferritic grains far from F/M interfaces or near F/F interfaces within a single phase ferritic Al-K steel ( Chamma et al., 2025 ), where the increase in nanohardness is absent or much less pronounced, as reported in  Table 1  and in  Fig. 5 .

These experimental results are similar to those obtained by  Delincé et al. (2006)  in fine-grained DP steels showing the interactions between the indented zone and the various features of the microstructure. The non-monotonic behavior observed in  Fig. 7  was also reported in previous nanoindentation studies near grain boundaries of pure FCC and BCC metals ( Almasri and Voyiadjis, 2010; Voyiadjis and Peters, 2010; Voyiadjis and Zhang, 2015; Zhang and Voyiadjis, 2016 ). This hardening behavior clearly indicates that microstructural heterogeneities (grain and phase boundaries) strongly influence the local nanohardness response. Here, F/M interfaces act as effective barriers to dislocation motion, confining plasticity and promoting the accumulation of GNDs. The result is an enhanced spatially localized strain hardening that modifies the classic ISE.  Fig. 8  schematically summarizes these trends. A classic ISE ( Nix and Gao, 1998 ) is found when indenting in a homogeneous region (yellow curve) and a non-monotonic hardness response with a characteristic “hump” is observed when indenting near an interface (purple curve) ( Voyiadjis and Peters, 2010; Voyiadjis and Zhang, 2015; Xiao et al., 2017 ).

To model the specific behavior observed in  Fig. 7  for this DP steel, we need to consider the modification of the classic ISE in the presence of an interface located at a certain distance

This model introduces a non-local formulation of the equivalent plastic strain to describe the size-dependent mechanical behavior observed at small scales. It captures the influence of GNDs, which arise from plastic strain gradients ( Ashby, 1970; Fleck et al., 1994 ). Here, GNDs are due to both the indentation loading at the origin of plastic strain gradients leading to the ISE, and GNDs pile-up originating from the presence of the F/M interface as a strong barrier to dislocation motion. Under nanoindentation loading, the highly localized deformation beneath the indenter induces a plastic zone with GNDs as shown in  Fig. 9 . GND densities increase as the deformation volume decreases, making it essential to incorporate plastic strain gradient effects into constitutive models at small scales. Besides, these GNDs also serve as obstacles to further dislocation motion, contributing to additional strain-hardening.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study demonstrates that Dual-Phase (DP) steels exhibit a local size dependent hardening in the presence of ferrite/martensite (F/M) interfaces. Nanohardness measurements reveal two distinct regimes depending on the distance between indentation and F/M interface: (i) a classical indentation size effect (ISE) when indentation loading is performed far away from F/M interfaces, where hardness decreases monotonically with increasing depth, and (ii) a non-monotonic response when indentation loading is performed close to F/M interfaces, where a hardening stage arises from plastic strain gradients characterized by a high level of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density.

These results show that interface-driven plastic strain gradients act as a dominant mechanism dependent on the distance to the interface. They contrast with the classic ISE, which only depends on indentation depth. They are consistent with distinct regimes recently described in the literature as a “complex ISE type” ( Wang et al., 2025 ). To explain this characteristic hardening stage inherent to F/M interfaces, a simplified version of the strain gradient plasticity (SGP) theory proposed by Voyiadjis and co-workers ( Voyiadjis and Peters, 2010; Voyiadjis and Zhang, 2015; Voyiadjis and Yaghoobi, 2017; Voyiadjis and Song, 2019 ) was exploited and calibrated with our experimental data using only three fitting parameters. This model captures the plastic volume beneath the indent in ferrite, which is limited by the F/M interface.
